text: This thesis deals with the automatic classification of the top three leading causes of
preventable blindness namely Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD), Glaucoma, and
Diabetic Retinopathy (DR). The work endeavors to overcome the existing architecture
limitations which result in inter-class feature interference and failure in important severity
grades due to systematic issues and therefore proposes a Bio-Inspired Hierarchical Gating
Multi-Expert Fusion system (HG-MEF-Bio) that endeavors to obtain specialist-level
accuracy at a single inference, outputting a single eleven-class output. A methodology
based on an expert-then-fuse paradigm utilizing three benchmark datasets namely
EyePACS for DR, AMDNet for AMD and ORIGA for Glaucoma, with approximately
22,700 fundus images was devised. Three specific disease classification models
(EnhancedAMDModelBio, HybridGlaucomaModelBio and EnhancedDRModelBio) were
trained using hybrid architectures (ResNet-50, ViT-B/16, and EfficientNet-B4) that are
embedded within several bio-inspired algorithms such as the Firefly Algorithm, Genetic
Algorithm, Particle Swarm Optimisation, Artificial Bee Colony, Differential Evolution and
Grey Wolf Optimiser ensuring clinical reliability with the implementation of a
differentiable Expected Calibration Error (ECE) loss. The proposed system achieved an
expert model accuracy of 97.25% for AMD, 95.45% for Glaucoma and 93.6% for DR
while improving the detection of Severe DR class by 39.3%-92.8%. The HG-MEF-Bio
model obtained a validation accuracy and macro-F1 score of 95.14% and 0.9278
respectively and outperforming current state-of-the-art. This thesis is one of the first few
approaches which implement a combination of different bio-inspired algorithms within a
training loop to perform classification of retinal images. Future works include clinical
validation and system deployment for tele-ophthalmology.

text: Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD)
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: AMD is a progressive, chronic and degenerative disease of the macula that affects more
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: than 50 years old people. It is one of the leading causes of irreversible vision loss among
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: older people in the developed world, affecting 196 million people in the world, and is
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: expected to reach 288 million in 2040. The main characteristic of AMD is that extracellular
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: deposits (drusen) accumulate between the RPE and Bruch's membrane, causing metabolic
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: defects of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and in the flow between the choriocapillaris
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: and the photoreceptors. This results in an progressive atropy of RPE and loss of
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: photoreceptors.
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: There are two types of AMD. The most common one is Dry AMD (geographic atropy)
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: which accounts for 85-90% of the AMD cases, characterized by soft and confluent drusen
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: and an atropy of RPE, while Wet AMD (neovascular AMD) accounts for the 10-15% cases,
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: and is responsible for about 90% of severe vision loss associated with AMD, is due to sub-
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: RPE neovascular membrane that leak, proliferate and bleed, leading to retinal edema,
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: haemorrhages and rapid photoreceptor death, and which can be stabilized or partially
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: reverted by anti-VEGF therapy when the disease is at its earlier stages.
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: When visualized on a fundus photograph, AMD presents several signs: hard and soft
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: drusen (yellowish spots, small and large with sharp/blurry borders), zones of
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: hypopigmentation and hyperpigmentation of the RPE, areas of geographic atrophy, and in
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: wet AMD the presence of fluid or haemorrhage under the retina, as well as neovascular
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: membranes. The fact that AMD has a complex and various aspect on fundus image in
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: different types and stages made it a challenging classification object for automatic system.
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: Glaucoma is the most common cause of irreversible blindness in the world and has afflicted
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: approximately 76 million individuals currently, with the figure predicted to increase to
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: more than 111 million by the year 2040. The principal difference to AMD is that whilst
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: central vision is impaired with AMD, glaucoma causes progressive neuronal cell death in
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

text: the RGCs and subsequent axonal degeneration, yielding characteristic patterns of visual
section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

section_heading: 1.1.2 Retinal Anatomy and the Pathophysiology of Target Diseases

section_heading: 1.1.3 Conventional Diagnostic Methods and Their Limitations

text: or slit lamp biomicroscopic examination by a human ophthalmologist or optometrist skilled
section_heading: 1.1.3 Conventional Diagnostic Methods and Their Limitations

text: in retinal diseases. While a human specialist provides highly accurate diagnoses when
section_heading: 1.1.3 Conventional Diagnostic Methods and Their Limitations

text: expertly employed, it is limited by a series of structural problems which prevents the ability
section_heading: 1.1.3 Conventional Diagnostic Methods and Their Limitations

text: to scale, access and standardize diagnoses on a population level:
section_heading: 1.1.3 Conventional Diagnostic Methods and Their Limitations

text: Firstly, the total number of ophthalmologists in the world is hopelessly undersubscribed
section_heading: 1.1.3 Conventional Diagnostic Methods and Their Limitations

text: relative to need, particularly in LMICs. WHO estimates there is a deficit of over 200,000
section_heading: 1.1.3 Conventional Diagnostic Methods and Their Limitations

text: ophthalmologists in the world, the most extreme being in those regions suffering the largest
section_heading: 1.1.3 Conventional Diagnostic Methods and Their Limitations

text: disease burden. Take for example, India; there are more than 80 million diabetics but less
section_heading: 1.1.3 Conventional Diagnostic Methods and Their Limitations

text: than 20,000 registered ophthalmic practitioners, giving a ratio of just one for about 4000
section_heading: 1.1.3 Conventional Diagnostic Methods and Their Limitations

text: patients at risk. Inevitable structural shortages such as these do not lend themselves to a
section_heading: 1.1.3 Conventional Diagnostic Methods and Their Limitations

text: screening strategy based on human interpretation and review. Secondly, even with the help
section_heading: 1.1.3 Conventional Diagnostic Methods and Their Limitations

text: of formal grading schemes (Wisconsin Grading System), experienced ophthalmologists
section_heading: 1.1.3 Conventional Diagnostic Methods and Their Limitations

text: judging DR grading have yielded as low as 60–80%. Issues such as visual subjectivity,
section_heading: 1.1.3 Conventional Diagnostic Methods and Their Limitations

text: fatiguing of screening ophthalmologists performing large volumes of checks and lack of
section_heading: 1.1.3 Conventional Diagnostic Methods and Their Limitations

text: ability to deal with marginal cases can all be potential causes.
section_heading: 1.1.3 Conventional Diagnostic Methods and Their Limitations

text: Thirdly, conventional screening is resource-intensive in both time and financial cost. An

section_heading: 1.1.3 Conventional Diagnostic Methods and Their Limitations

section_heading: 1.1.3 Conventional Diagnostic Methods and Their Limitations

section_heading: 1.1.3 Conventional Diagnostic Methods and Their Limitations

section_heading: 1.1.3 Conventional Diagnostic Methods and Their Limitations

text: Most current automated retinal disease systems are disease-specific: either classifying DR
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text: alone, or AMD alone, or Glaucoma alone, being trained and tested on samples held out
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text: from the same distribution, and tested on data which originates from the same disease-
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text: specific dataset. Whilst these single-disease systems perform well within their given scope,
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text: they do not reflect the reality of clinical screening: a given patient could be afflicted with
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text: multiple retinal conditions simultaneously; it is desired that all screening must start from
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text: the same fundus camera/screening visit and perform triage across all diseases.
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text: To overcome these shortcomings, several multi-disease approaches have been proposed,
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text: where systems are trained to perform multiple tasks simultaneously. When a single deep
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text: neural network is trained to perform multiple classification tasks at the same time, then
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text: there is a possibility of inter-class interference of feature representations: The
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text: representations learnt for AMD classification may be counter-productive for DR grading
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text: in the latter layers of the network, where discrimination is based upon subtle patterns in
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text: retinal images. The problem is aggravated by a domain shift that usually occurs between
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text: separate disease-specific data-sets (acquired from different imaging systems, patient
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text: cohorts and clinical sites).
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text: thesis addresses this challenge through an expert-then-fuse paradigm: three disease-
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text: specific expert models are independently trained on their respective disease datasets,
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text: developing specialised and maximally discriminative feature representations for each
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text: condition, before being unified through a learned hierarchical fusion network. This
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text: architecture preserves the benefits of disease-specific specialisation whilst enabling cross-
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text: disease interaction through the fusion layer's cross-attention mechanism — producing a
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text: system that is both more accurate at the individual disease level and more clinically
section_heading: 1.1.7 Multi-Disease Classification: The Case for Expert Fusion

text: comprehensive at the system level.

text: The scope of the current study is set as the design, implementation, training, evaluation,
and interpretability study of a multi-disease classification system on retinal fundus images
which aims to diagnose AMD, Glaucoma, and Diabetic Retinopathy. This study includes
all steps of the deep learning pipeline starting from input images through data
preprocessing, data augmentation, training of expert model, implementation of bio-inspired
algorithm, training of fusion network, post-training optimization and evaluation in both
qualitative and quantitative ways.
Specifically, the scope includes the following dimensions:
• Imaging modality: Only two-dimensional colour fundus photography (CFP) is used
for this study, which is also the most common and affordable retinal imaging
modality in population screening programs. OCT and fluorescein angiography are
important but not discussed as part of this work, however, the architecture is
extensible to include these imaging modalities.
• Disease Taxonomy :For AMD four types (AMD, Cataract, Diabetes and Normal)
are taken in consideration, For Glaucoma two types (Referable Glaucoma, Non
Referable Glaucoma), for DR five types (No DR, Mild NPDR, Moderate NPDR,
Severe NPDR, Proliferative DR). So total 11 classes in fusion module at
Architecture 2 and 12 at architecture 1 with inclusion of multiple.
• Sources of the dataset: We utilized publicly available retinal images datasets:
EyePACS and APTOS for DR, AMDNet and HYAMD for AMD and REFUGE
and ORIGA for Glaucoma, all are used in the peer reviewed literature as
benchmarks of retinal AI. This ensures comparability.
• Algorithmic Scope: It combines six bio-inspired optimisation algorithms FA,
GWO, GA, PSO, ABC, DE as the core parts of the training pipeline alongside the
traditional deep learning components such as ResNet-50, ViT-B/16, EfficientNet-
B4, CBAM, FocalLoss, mixed-precision training.
• The metrics that were considered were: Classification accuracy, macro and
weighted F1-score, AUC-ROC, Matthews Correlation Coefficient, bio-algorithm
convergence analysis, ECE calibration analysis, Grad-CAM explanation analysis.
• Computation: All the training is performed on GPU based computation
infrastructure (NVIDIA T4 and RTX A4000) with PyTorch deep learning
framework, using reproducible Python modular scripts.
It can be noted from the above, that a full design and test has been carried out here and it
is possible to note certain limitations within it which define the limits of this work and
propose future research areas:
• Dataset Scale and Variation: While the datasets used are typical benchmarks found
in the retinal AI literature, they don't show the full extent of variation that exists in
fundus images based on Ethnicity, Acquisition Device and Clinic type. Most
importantly the minority classes of DR severity are still too small to train deep
learning, the most frequent, despite the most potent data augmentation techniques,
real-life additional clinical data.
• Constraint on Imaging modality: It was decided to use only color fundus
photograph based on their availability in LMICs, use of fundus photography in tele-
ophthalmology applications and their prevalence. However it also implies that the
system we developed doesn't utilize information available from OCT and FA.
Specifically OCT has been extremely useful in AMD grading since it directly
allows visualization of RPE, drusen, CNV in 3D.
• Handling of comorbidities: Currently, this system considers AMD, Glaucoma and
DR as completely separate disease in classification sense, based on the assumption
that in expert-then-fuse architecture the model only predicts one primary diagnosis
for each image. However in a real-world situation a patient might suffer from more
than one disease at the same time i.e., Glaucoma and DR. The proposed architecture
does not allow multiple labels for output and that would be the most logical addition
for further work.
• HG-MEF-Bio Fusion Training status: As of the time of writing the HG-MEF-Bio

text: This is one of the most rapidly developing areas of medical AI within the past ten years;
fueled by large-scale annotated datasets of fundus images, the emergence of powerful deep
learning architectures, and a vital clinical need for a system supporting scaled screening.
In this literature review, we consolidate 33 research papers and pre-prints published within
the last five years (2020-2025) into 6 main clusters: 1) CNN-based automated retinal
disease classification; 2) Vision Transformers and CNN-ViT hybrids; 3) multi-disease and
multi-label retinal screening; 4) ensembles in retinal screening; 5) attention mechanisms
for retinal feature extraction; and 6) bio-inspired optimization in medical imaging. Finally,
the literature review ends with a summary table and categorical list of current research gaps
which are the direct motivation behind the innovative network architectures that can be
seen in HG-MEF and HG-MEF-Bio below. The structuring of this literature review reflects
the timeline of this field as it developed from single-disease, single model to multi-disease,
hybrid, and ensemble solutions, and eventually to bio-inspired search methods; this
temporal progression represents more than time passing; rather, it marks a recognition of
specific obstacles in this field such as class imbalance, intra-class feature impurity, domain
shifts, and clinical trust.
The foundational era of deep learning-based retinal disease classification was dominated
by Convolutional Neural Networks, which demonstrated the feasibility of replacing hand-
crafted feature engineering with end-to-end learned representations. This category of work
establishes the performance baselines against which the more sophisticated architectures
in subsequent sections are evaluated.
Andrab and Gupta [1] produced a systematic review on the state-of-the-art in deep learning
and classical machine learning techniques to classify Diabetic Retinopathy using fundus
images. This study found techniques ranging from texture based SVMs to ResNet and
DenseNet implemented on EyePACS and Messidor datasets. It was noted that in terms of
DR grading, a consistent performance plateau of approximately 90-92% accuracy was seen
from single model CNN implementations which was due to "both intra-class variations of
retinal lesion morphology and ambiguity in distinguishing adjacent severity grades".
Importantly it was found that systems commonly available in publications failed on the
task of diagnosing Severe NPDR.This is also of relevance as it bears a direct relation to
Architecture 1 result in the present study, thus indicating the endurance of the minority
Archana et al [3] utilized a DenseNet based transfer learning approach to classify the
different severities of DR across multi-class classification using APTOS dataset, achieving
an overall accuracy of 94.2 percent. The study demonstrated the value of dense skip
connections in preserving fine-grained feature information from early network layers — a
design principle that influenced the multi-backbone architecture of the expert models in
the present work. However, the study did not address the minority class imbalance
problem, and the reported per-class breakdown reveals accuracy on Severe DR and
Proliferative DR substantially below the overall figure.

extracted from fundus images for DR classification and reported a maximum accuracy of

text: Bio-inspired optimisation algorithms have been applied to medical imaging tasks across a
spectrum of applications — from feature selection and hyperparameter tuning to
architecture search and post-training calibration. The review of this literature reveals a
consistent pattern: existing applications are predominantly applied to shallow machine
learning pipelines or as post-hoc optimisation steps on pre-trained deep networks, rather
than as fully integrated training-loop mechanisms operating within deep learning systems.
Singh et al. [29] applied a customised Particle Swarm Optimisation algorithm (CPSO) to
the feature selection problem in Glaucoma classification, using PSO to identify the optimal
subset of handcrafted morphological features (optic disc area, CDR, rim width) from a
larger feature set, before feeding the selected features to four classical machine learning
classifiers (SVM, KNN, Decision Tree, Random Forest). The study achieved 94.2 percent
accuracy on the DRISHTI-GS dataset. Whilst demonstrating the utility of PSO for
navigating high-dimensional feature spaces, the work is fundamentally limited by its
reliance on handcrafted features: the PSO optimisation cannot access the richer,
hierarchically learned representations of deep networks. The present work extends PSO's
role from feature selection on handcrafted features to in-training decision threshold
optimisation and post-training boundary calibration within deep expert models — a
qualitatively different and more powerful application.
The variants of the Artificial Bee Colony algorithm applied on medical image processing
were reviewed in the paper of ozturk et al. [30] that presents a review on the applications
for medical image segmentation, registration and feature extraction. The survey
systematically documented the performance advantages of ABC-based approaches over
traditional gradient descent in non-convex, multi-modal optimisation landscapes typical of
medical image processing — particularly for problems with discrete or discontinuous
search spaces where gradient-based methods are inapplicable. The survey's identification
of ABC's strengths in routing and allocation problems — modelling expert honey-source
allocation through Employed, Onlooker, and Scout bee phases — directly informed the
present work's deployment of ABC for the fusion routing bias optimisation in the
ABCGatedRoutingNetwork.
Gao et al. [31] presented a modified ABC algorithm hybridised with Differential Evolution
to enhance precision and convergence rate on numerical optimisation benchmarks from the
CEC suite. The study demonstrated that the ABC-DE hybrid achieved superior
performance over either algorithm in isolation, particularly in mid-dimensional search
spaces (10 to 50 dimensions) — the dimensionality range that corresponds to the expert
routing bias (3-dimensional), cross-attention blend weights (3-dimensional), and feature
scaling factors (3-dimensional) optimised in the present work's fusion model. The
algorithmic finding that ABC and DE are complementary — ABC providing exploration
through bee colony diversity and DE providing exploitation through differential mutation
— directly motivated their simultaneous deployment at the fusion level of HG-MEF-Bio.
The PSO-Enhanced Ensemble DNN work [32] applied PSO to the optimisation of learning
rate and momentum hyperparameters of a deep neural network ensemble for optic disc
segmentation, achieving 89.7 percent Dice coefficient on the DRISHTI dataset.  PSO in
deep learning training is still in its infancy in this study-the method was used to optimize
the global training rate and momentum ( hyperparameters which are common to all layers).
This work extends the use of PSO in deep learning significantly by applying it to per-class
decision thresholds (an off-line optimization applied to a task specific aspect of the decision
process) and applying it as an in-training loss function modifier via the
ThresholdPenaltyLoss, a module that shapes the learned representations.

text: In this paper, a hierarchy multi-expert fusion system is proposed for automated and
simultaneous detection of three main retinal diseases (AMD, Glaucoma, and DR) in
color fundus image. The top level framework is the expert-then-fuse paradigm, in which
three expert deep learning models were individually trained for each disease using the
individual data set and the trained models are fused into an ensemble learned fusion
network to output a single multi-disease classification. The framework deliberately
avoids the inter-class feature collision as in naive combined single model architecture.
In the naive single model approach, multiple disease supervision signals compete for
the gradients from back-propagation, and therefore "hurts" the expertise of the
individual model.
The system is delivered as two complete architectures. Architecture 1 — the
Hierarchical Gating Multi-Expert Fusion (HG-MEF) — employs standard deep
learning components without bio-inspired optimisation, establishing a rigorous non-bio
baseline. In this Architecture 2 (Bio-Inspired HG-MEF-Bio) each non-differentiable
architectural choice present in Architecture 1 was substituted and supported by one or
more bio-inspired metaheuristics algorithms working at: attention weight optimization,
loss function parameters evolution, decision threshold tuning, fusion routing fine-
tuning, and feature contribution weights. By using these two architectures we could
show controlled ablation of the bio-inspired mechanisms and a quantifiable
contribution of each and all of them.
Architecture 1 consists of four trained models: EnhancedAMDModel (4 classes),
HybridGlaucomaModel (2 classes), HybridDRModel (5 classes), and the
HierarchicalMultiExpertFusion network (12 unified classes). The three expert models
are trained independently on their respective datasets. Upon completion, their backbone
weights are frozen and the HG-MEF fusion network is trained on top of their outputs.
The unified taxonomy comprises twelve classes: Normal, AMD, Cataract, NRG, RG,
DRNone, DRMild, DRModerate, DRSevere, DR_Proliferative, Diabetes, Multiple.
Architecture 2 is similar to Architecture 1 but with bio-augmented experts
(EnhancedAMDModelBio, HybridGlaucomaModelBio, EnhancedDRModelBio)
instead of three expert models, and HierarchicalBioExpertFusion (HG-MEF-Bio) is
used instead of the fusion network. It produces eleven merged classes (the 'Multiple'
class is excluded from the mutually exclusive taxonomy). In this architecture, six bio-
inspired algorithms (FA, GWO, GA, PSO, ABC and DE) were incorporated throughout
the training process, at all levels of the architecture. A three separate DR solutions were
incorporated, the DR1, DR2, and DR3, in order to address the most crucial issue of
failure in the minority class in Architecture 1.

corresponding to one disease domain. All datasets contain two-dimensional colour
fundus photographs of the posterior pole of the eye. Table 3.1 Is a summary of dataset

The AMD dataset has 4 classes; AMD(drusen deposits; atrophy of the RPE; subretinal
fluid in wet AMD), Cataract(lens opacity appearing as reduced contrast and haziness),
Diabetes(early diabetic involvement of the macula not necessarily graded for the
severity of DR), and Normal (healthy fundus). The dataset is already divided into the
train, validation and test set folders, with roughly equivalent proportions of each class
(approx. 100 samples per class in the validation set). This 4 class taxonomy has been
generated according to the typical branches seen in a screening setting in a general
ophthalmology clinic.
Glaucoma data has a binary referral classification Non-Referable Glaucoma (NRG) and
Referable Glaucoma (RG), which corresponds to the actual screening process (refer to
Specialist if RG, continue routine follow up if NRG), CDR 0.6; neuroretinal rim
notching; RNFL thinning. Approx 385 samples per class in the validation set. In other
words, it's an unbalanced binary problem.
For the DR dataset, there are five classes: NoDR, mildNPDR, moderateNPDR,
severeNPDR, and proliferativeDR. This highly imbalanced distribution (NoDR:Severe
ratio is 10:1), reflects true clinical screening proportions, is the main algorithmic hurdle
for which the 3 DR specific approaches in Architecture 2 is targeting. Dataset Custom
split script is used to have even class distribution between train (70%), validation (15%)
and test (15%) with fix seed of 42.
Preprocessing removes large variations present across the set of retinal images due to
illumination conditions, camera models and zoom settings of field of view, as well as
differences in image quality - significant variations found in clinical sets of images.
Two different preprocessing pipeline were established, each tuned to the features for
specific disease identification.
The Ben Graham preprocessing technique is derived from the winning method of
Kaggle's Diabetic Retinopathy detection competition and consists of seven steps that
remove global illumination variations and local lesion contrast. Let I denote the raw
input image as a three-channel matrix I ∈ ℝ^(H×W×3).
Step 1: Gaussian Blur and Thresholding
Image is blurred using Gaussian blur with kernel size of 55. Then, thresholding is
applied on blurred image to obtain binary mask M.
M(x,y) = 1 if GaussianBlur(I)(x,y) > 10 else 0 (3.1)
Step 2: Morphological Operations
Morphological closing followed by opening is applied to M using an elliptical
structuring element of size 15×15 pixels. Let ⊕ denote dilation, ⊖ erosion, ∘ opening,
M_refined = (M • SE) ∘ SE    where SE = ELLIPSE(15×15) (3.2)
Step 3: Circular Crop
The minimum enclosing circle of the largest contour in M_refined is computed,
yielding centre (cx, cy) and radius r. A circular mask C is applied:
C(x,y) = 1 if (x − cx)² + (y − cy)² ≤ r²  else 0 (3.3)
The image is multiplied by C (background set to black), then cropped to the bounding
rectangle [cx−r, cx+r] × [cy−r, cy+r] and resized to 512×512 pixels using area
interpolation (INTER_AREA).
Step 4: Light correction
The differences due to local light are eliminated by subtracting a greatly blurred image
from the original one, once the image has been scaled to keep the mean intensity value:
I_out = α·I + β·GaussianBlur(I, σ=10) + γ (3.4)
where α = 4 , β = −4 , and γ = 128 . This represents a high pass filter: you remove the
background global illumination (with large-blur) and are left with the variation of local
contrast around retinal lesions. Constant = 128 allows the image to be adjusted to grey-
level, avoiding clipping artifacts.
Glaucoma grading is highly dependent on the cup-to-disc ratio (CDR) which is the ratio
of the vertical cup diameter to the optic disc. The CDR can be affected by the global
illumination correction used. Ben Graham method applies a variable bright adjustment
over the space, this can change the apparent CDR and create a grading artefact. Hence
the Glaucoma preprocessing pipeline does not include illumination correction and uses
CLAHE applied only on the green channel.
Step 1: Retina Masking
Identical circular masking to Steps 1–3 of the Ben Graham pipeline: threshold → largest
contour → minEnclosingCircle → circular mask + crop → resize 512×512.
Step 2: CLAHE on Green Channel
The green channel G belongs to R raise to (512x512) is extracted from the preprocessed
image. CLAHE is applied with  a clip limit of L = 2.0 and tile grid size T = 8×8 is
The clip limit L limits the amplification of noise in the low-contrast regions, by clipping
the histogram of each tile before it's repartitioned. The green channel is selected,
because the optic disc and cup are in maximum contrast in green color, compared to
red and blue, and hemoglobin absorption feature is prominent in the green spectral

The proposed system does not employ handcrafted feature engineering. Instead, feature
representations are learned end-to-end by the deep neural network components.
However, three principled feature shaping mechanisms guide what features the models
learn to extract: multi-backbone ensemble feature learning, gradient-weighted class
activation mapping (GradCAM) for saliency-guided channel attention, and cross-
attention for inter-branch feature selection.
All the expert models consist of three parallel backbone networks capable of extracting
the complementary features. While ResNet-50 extracts the local spatial hierarchical
features, such as edges, textures and morphological shapes via convolutions with
incrementally increased receptive field, the ViT-B/16 is the global relational feature
extractor by performing attention over the whole patches of the image at the same time.
EfficientNet-B4 learns lesion-scale detail features at a resolution (380×380)
intermediate between the two. The three 768-dimensional feature vectors produced by
the backbones constitute three complementary feature spaces that are subsequently
fused through cross-attention.
In Architecture 2, the EfficientNet-B4 lesion branch is augmented with Gradient-
weighted Class Activation Mapping (GradCAM) to guide bio-inspired channel
attention optimisation. GradCAM computes the importance α_k^c of each feature map
channel k for class c through global average pooling of the gradients of the class score
with respect to the feature map activations:
where y^c is the class score before softmax, A^k_{ij} is the activation at position (i,j)
of feature map channel k, and Z = H × W is the number of spatial locations. The saliency
map L^c_GradCAM is computed as:
L^c_GradCAM = ReLU( Σ_k α_k^c · A^k ) (3.8)
The mean activation of L^c_GradCAM serves as the brightness signal b in the Firefly
Algorithm fitness function, guiding channel attention weight selection toward
configurations that attend to diagnostically relevant retinal regions.
Cross-attention performs learnable feature selection across the three backbone
representations. Given feature vectors from two branches — Q (query) and K, V (key-
value) — the cross-attention mechanism computes:
CrossAttn(Q, K, V) = softmax( QK^T / √d_k ) · V (3.9)
where d_k is the key dimension (96 per head in 8-head attention). This allows each
branch to selectively attend to — and therefore incorporate — features from the other
branches that are most relevant to its own representation. In the 8-head variant
(GWOUnifiedCrossAttention), the 768-dimensional feature vectors are linearly
projected into 8 subspaces of 96 dimensions each, with separate W_Q, W_K, W_V
projection matrices per head:
MultiHead(Q,K,V) = Concat(head_1, ..., head_8) · W_O (3.10)
head_i = CrossAttn(QW_Q^i, KW_K^i, VW_V^i) (3.11)

The AMD expert employs MultiWayCrossAttention across all six pairwise directions

f_cross = CrossAttn(Q=f_ViT, K=f_CNN, V=f_CNN) (3.17)

Head_1: LN(f) → Linear(768→512) → GELU → Dropout(p=0.3) →
Head_2: CBAM(f) → LN → Linear(768→512) → ReLU → Dropout(p=0.3)

cross-attention streams separately.
Genetic Algorithm (GA) — Class Weight Evolution
The GA evolves a population of n = 20 weight vectors W = [w_1, w_2, ..., w_C] ∈
ℝ^C over 8 generations using tournament selection (k = 3), single-point crossover (rate
= 0.70), Gaussian mutation (σ = 0.3, rate = 0.15), and elitism (best individual always
For the DR model, the fitness function incorporates a recall-floor constraint (SOL2):
Fitness(W) = F_macro(W) − 2.0 · Σ_c max(0, τ − recall_c(W)) + 0.1 ·
Σ_{c ∈ H} recall_c(W) (3.39)
where τ = 0.55 is the minimum acceptable recall per class, H = {Mild, Proliferative,
Severe} is the set of hard classes, and F_macro is macro-averaged F1. No_DR weight
is hard-clamped to [0.5, 1.5] to prevent majority-class dominance. GA runs every
GA_INTERVAL ∈ {5, 8} epochs on the full validation set.
Particle Swarm Optimisation (PSO) — Per-Class Decision Thresholds
PSO maintains a swarm of n = 30 particles, each representing a C-dimensional
threshold vector θ ∈ [0.05, 0.95]^C. Each particle has a position θ_i and velocity v_i.
The update equations are:
v_i(t+1) = w · v_i(t) + c_1·r_1·(pbest_i − θ_i) + c_2·r_2·(gbest − θ_i) (3.40)
with inertia w = 0.7 , cognitive coefficient c_1 = 1.5 , social coefficient c_2 = 1.5 , and
r_1, r_2 ~ U(0,1) . The FN-aware fitness function prioritises recall:
Fitness(θ) = mean_F1(θ) + 3.0 · mean_recall(θ) (3.42)
PSO runs post-training on the full validation set for 100 iterations. For DR, an
additional in-training SOL1 PSO runs every 10 epochs; the optimised thresholds θ_PSO
are then converted to a training loss:
L_SOL1 = λ_PSO · mean( ReLU( θ_PSO[y] − p_y ) ) (3.43)
where p_y is the predicted probability of the correct class y and λ_PSO = 0.2 . This
penalises the model whenever its confidence on the correct class falls below the PSO-
optimised threshold, co-evolving model confidence and decision boundaries.
Artificial Bee Colony (ABC) — Fusion Routing Bias Correction
ABC optimises a 3-dimensional routing bias vector b ∈ [−1.5, 1.5]^3 that shifts the
gate logits of the ABCGatedRoutingNetwork. A colony of 20 bees (10 employed, 10
onlooker) searches the bias space:
Employed bee phase: each employed bee i exploits its source b_i by generating a
If b_new improves fitness (validation accuracy on 5-batch subset), it replaces b_i;
otherwise the failure counter for source i is incremented.
Onlooker bee phase: onlookers select sources proportionally to their fitness:
P_i = fitness_i / Σ_k fitness_k (3.45)
Scout bee phase: if source i stagnates for limit = 5 consecutive trials, it is abandoned
and replaced by a randomly generated new source b_i ~ U(−1.5, 1.5)^3. ABC runs
every 8 epochs during fusion training.
Differential Evolution (DE/rand/1/bin) — Expert Feature Contribution Weights
DE maintains a population of n = 30 vectors, each representing 3-dimensional feature
scaling weights w ∈ [0.01, 1.0]^3 (softmax-normalised before use). For each target
vector x_i, a mutant vector v_i is created using three randomly selected distinct vectors
x_r1, x_r2, x_r3:
A trial vector u_i is created through binomial crossover:
u_{i,j} = v_{i,j}  if rand_j(0,1) < CR  else x_{i,j},    CR = 0.9 (3.47)
Greedy selection: if fitness(u_i) ≥ fitness(x_i), replace x_i with u_i; otherwise retain
x_i. DE runs every 6 epochs during fusion training over 20 generations.
SOL1: PSO-in-Training (DR Expert Only)
SOL1 is the first of three dedicated solutions to the DR minority class problem. In
standard practice, PSO is applied post-training as a threshold calibration step. SOL1
extends this by incorporating PSO-optimised thresholds directly into the training loss
during the DR expert model training, creating a co-evolutionary feedback loop between
the model and the PSO optimiser.
Every 10 training epochs, a PSO run is executed on a small validation subset to find the
current best per-class decision thresholds θ_PSO ∈ ℝ^5 for the five DR classes. These
thresholds are then used to define an additional training loss that penalises the model
whenever its predicted probability for the correct class falls below the corresponding
L_SOL1 = λ_SOL1 · mean_i( ReLU( θ_PSO[y_i] − p_{y_i} ) )
where y_i is the true class label for sample i, p_{y_i} is the predicted softmax
probability for that class, and θ_PSO[y_i] is the PSO-optimised threshold for class
y_i. The ReLU operator only allows the loss to fire when the model is not confident
about its prediction (under threshold); if it is overconfident on a correct prediction there
is no penalty. We introduced a loss co-efficient SO L1 = 0.2 to trade off this penalty
with the normal classfication losses. This mechanism whereby PSO determines
thresholds for the current weakness of the model, and these thresholds cause the model
to become more confident on the minority class(es), are the reason for the Huge increase
of Severe DR accuracy from 39.3% to 92.8%
SOL2: GA Recall-Floor Penalty (DR Expert Only)
SOL2 modifies the Genetic Algorithm fitness function used for class weight
evolutionto incorporate a hard recall floor constraint and a hard-class recall bonus. In
Architecture 1, fixed class weights [1.0, 2.0, 1.5, 3.0, 3.5] for the five DR classes are
insufficient to prevent the model from sacrificing minority class recall in favour of
overall accuracy — a consequence of the 10:1 imbalance between No_DR  and
Severe SOL2 replaces the standard macro-F1 GA fitness with a clinically informed
composite fitness function:
Fitness(ω) = MacroF1(ω) − 2.0 · Σ_k max(0, 0.55 − recall_k(ω)) + 0.1 · Σ_{j ∈ H}
Where 5 is the class weight vector being evolved, recallk() is the per class recall on the
validation set obtained using these weights and H = {Mild, Proliferative, Severe} is the
set of hard minority classes. The first term is the objective, the second is a lower bound
on recall, at which any class whose recall is below 0.55, loses 2 points for every
percentage point that its recall is below 0.55, making it the strongest penalty and thus
dominating (20 greater than the hard class bonus), while the third term acts as a reward
for further increasing recall on the three hardest classes. As an extra condition, the
NoDR weight has been clamped at 1.5. This stops the GA from collapsing the dominant
NoDR weight to 0, a degenerate solution, while still maximizing minority class fitness,
thus satisfying the clinical condition that NoDR class must always be classified
correctly The GA class weights evolved by SOL2 reached values of up to 4.9 for the
Severe class across different GA runs, compared to the fixed weight of 3.5 in
Architecture 1.

text: All experiments from both phase-I and phase-II were performed on GPU-accelerated
computing hardware. The Phase-I training was performed using Google Colab Pro (on an
NVIDIA Tesla T4 16GB VRAM) and the GPU offered enough throughput to execute both
single-model CNN and Vision Transformer training pipelines. Phase-II training was
performed on a local machine with an NVIDIA RTX A4000 16GB VRAM allowing to run
the 3-backbone Architecture 2 experts without losing any state with a complete checkpoint
persistence strategy and with the required bfloat16 Automatic Mixed Precision.
The software stack used was based on python 3.12 and Pytorch 2.0+ as the core deep
learning framework. The other major libraries include: torchvision for general image
transforms, Albumentations for creating disease-specific augmentations pipeline,
timm(PyTorch Image Models) to obtain pre-trained ViT-B/16 and EfficientNet-B4
backbone for initialization, scikit-learn for AUC-ROC and classification report calculation,
and Matplotlib and Seaborn for visualizing the training curve and convergence. All the
model checkpoint files for Phase-II used an atomic write-verify-replace (writing to .pth.tmp
and then only if correct loading was successful writing to .pth by rename) mechanism to
reduce likelihood of checkpoint corruption on long training sessions. Custom function for
cleaning the state-dictionary keys were implemented to remove origmod. Prefix coming
from calling torch.compile() in Colab when models of Phase-I were moved to VS code
All three of the repositories available for public access were used over the two project
stages. Both of the EyePACS and APTOS 2019 datasets were used for Diabetic
Retinopathy (DR), which contains fundus images for five classification categories; no
DR, mild NPDR, moderate NPDR, severe NPDR and proliferative DR. Both the
AMDNet and HYAMD repositories were used for Age-Related Macular Degeneration
(AMD), which has four classification categories; AMD, Cataract, Diabetes and Normal.
Both of the REFUGE and ORIGA benchmark datasets were used for Glaucoma which
was classified into two binary labels; Non-Referable Glaucoma (NRG) and Referable
In phase I, all three disease datasets were clubbed together into one directory, diseases
having their names prepended to filenames and divided 60/20/20 into
training/validation/test set keeping stratified class distributions of the datasets. In phase
II, datasets are kept individual to diseases and class distributions are 70/15/15 stratified
split. The validation sets had 400 samples for AMD (100 samples for each class), 770 for
Glaucoma (385 for each class) and 607 for the test set of DR (No_DR: 169, Mild: 108,
Moderate: 155, Proliferative: 106, Severe: 69). A radius validity check was performed in
the pre-processing to reject noisy images. Any fundus image where the detected radius
for retinal structure is less than 50 pixels was rejected for all splits.
A single preprocessing pipeline was utilized for all diseases in Phase-I. These included
automated circular retinal region cropping based on intensity thresholding, Ben-Graham
weighted subtraction using a Gaussian filter (sigma=10) for enhancing the vessels and
edges, extraction of green channel which contains the largest range of lesion pixels,
CLAHE for equalizing the local contrast and image size normalization to 224x224 and
384x384 for CNNs and Vision Transformer respectively.
There were three motivated medical preprocessing steps applied in Phase-II (one per
disease). For AMD and DR, the entire Ben-Graham pipeline was used with output
resolution 512 512. For Glaucoma, a new pipeline was built: retina masking using an
intensity threshold and largest contour detection followed by CLAHE on the green
channel only (clipLimit = 2.0, tileGridSize = 8) 8, skipping the illumination correction
step not to alter the cup-to-disk morphology which is the dominant symptom in glaucoma
classification. The augmentation policies were also specific for each disease: 2 (uniform)
for AMD, class-aware for DR using 3 for mild DR, 4 for severe and proliferative DR and
limited augmentation (horizontal flip, 5 rotation, 0.1 brightness) for Glaucoma as optic
disk morphology should not be changed.
For all the models, phases, and architectures the following evaluation metrics were used:
• Overall Accuracy: the accuracy of all class labels; it is the main summed up
• Per-Class accuracy: it is the accuracy of each of the classes (diagonal of the
confusion matrix), thus the performance of each minority class is taken into account
(e.g. Serious DR); it also represents the main figure for the evaluation of a specific
• Macro-averaged F1 Score: a per-class F1 Score averaged over all classes so that
each class has a weight. This is the target for optimizing the DR models since we
assume significant class imbalance.
• Weighted F1 score: an F1 Score averaged over each class with weight of samples
per class; this is an evaluation figure for imbalanced classes when a reduction in
class imbalance is not desired (thus can be used in a fusion model, because different
classes could likely have different number of training data).
• AUC-ROC (One-vs-Rest): area under the ROC curve, it evaluates class separation
performance independently of a threshold.
• Confusion Matrix: it is a specialized version for the purpose that it allows us to
identify systematically different kinds of errors between classes of different degree
• Bio-Algorithm Fitness: the results shown are the performance for each bio-inspired
algorithm for iterations; the FA fitness curve was monitored for a single run; the
best fitness achieved by the GWO population; the macro-F1 for GA for each run;
the weighted-F1 for PSO for each iteration.
For Phase-I training, five CNN architectures (VGG16, ResNet-50, DenseNet-121,
InceptionV3 and MobileNetV2) were trained using ImageNet-pretrained weights and a 10-
layer Vision Transformer (ViT-B/16). All the models were trained on the combined four-
class dataset (AMD, DR, Glaucoma, Healthy) in a 60-20-20 train/validation/test split. The
CNN models were trained with the Adam optimiser with the learning rate initially set to
25-40 epochs (depending on model performance and validation loss). The Vision

text: Phase-II Architecture 1 used an expert-then-fuse approach, where 3 disease specific expert
models were trained independently prior to training the fusion network. The AMD Expert
(EnhancedAMDModel) was trained using Adam (LR = 0.0001) and ReduceLROnPlateau
(triggered two times: 0.0001- 0.00005- 0.00003), with a batch size of 32, and early stopping
over 17 epochs. The Glaucoma Expert (HybridGlaucomaModel) was trained using Adam
and cost sensitive cross-entropy (RG class weight = 2.0) for 27 epochs. The DR Expert
(HybridDRModel) was trained using CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts and class weighted
cross-entropy (higher penalties for Severe, Mild, and Proliferative stages) for 17 epochs.
The HierarchicalMultiExpertFusion (HG-MEF) network was trained on top of the expert
models (with backbone fixed) over 30 epochs. The fusion loss combined FocalLoss
(gamma = 2) and GateDiversityLoss (an entropy regularization term on gate distributions,
to ensure they did not collapse), using ReduceLROnPlateau from LR=0.0001 to
LR~0.000001 over 30 epochs. The output taxonomy consisted of 12 aggregated classes,
spanning the 3 disease domains.
During the training of the expert via each loop on architecture 2, the AMD Bio Expert was
employed in place of the CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts LR schedule. The AMD Bio
Expert would update the channels of the EfficientNet-B4 each time FA+GradCAM was
called (which happened every 5 mini-batches), and the GWO cross attention blend weights
each validation epoch. The GA per-class loss weights were updated every 5 mini-batches,
and the post-training decision threshold was fine-tuned with PSO. The DR Bio Expert was
fully trained for 50 epochs using ReduceLROnPlateau on validation Macro-F1 (with
patience=5). This approach included three novel, DR-specific algorithms: SOL1 (a penalty
every 10 batches for being in-training with a lower decision threshold using PSO), SOL2
(a strict, floor on recall of 70% on each of the Severe, Mild, and Proliferative classes using
the GA, which ensures minimum recall performance), and SOL3
(RecallAwareDiversityLoss). For the Glaucoma Bio Expert, the networks (on the 3
backbones) were trained using AMP bfloat16 mixed-precision along with gradient
checkpointing in order to allow for an entire batch size of 16 within 16GB of VRAM. Also,
the HG-MEF-Bio fusion approach was utilized instead of the ABCGatedRoutingNetwork
gating network, the GWOUnifiedCrossAttention cross-attention module, and the
DEFeatureMixer feature mixing module.
Five CNN architectures were evaluated on the unified four-class retinal disease
classification task. The MobileNetV2 architecture performed the worst overall with 71%
overall accuracy and 0.50 macro F1 score, but it seemed to over-classify 'Healthy' across
all its predictions, this is likely due to class imbalance and the very restricted model.
VGG16 performed much better with 81% overall accuracy and a macro and weighted F1
of 0.82 and 0.83 respectively, showing excellent performance in 'DR' and 'Healthy' classes
but poorer precision in 'Glaucoma' while ResNet-50, DenseNet-121, InceptionV3 ranged
from 83%-88% accuracy overall. Every CNN architecture predicted "Healthy" with >90%
accuracy and "DR" with 75%-88% accuracy but the lower performance was with
"Glaucoma" and "AMD", the characteristics of which required spatial attention rather than
global textural analysis.
This standard 10-layer ViT-B/16 was trained for up to 120 epochs with cosine decay and
swarm-inspired attention sparsification and produced best of phase-I results, around 90-
91% in macro and weighted F1 scores of about 0.90, an excellent result. The confusion
matrix gave the accuracy 96% on Healthy, 84% on AMD, 82% on Mild DR and 78% on
Glaucoma. The attention in the Grad-CAM visualisations was anatomically relevant,
microaneurysms/haemorrhages for DR classifications, drusen deposits/ pigment changes
for AMD, and optic disc shape for Glaucoma. Despite producing an impressive aggregate
accuracy, the single ViT suffered from three structural weaknesses, and was taken forward
in Phase-II: 1) inter-class interference of features between AMD and Proliferative DR, as
there is a partial overlap in their visual characteristics; 2) lack of any coherent strategy to
address the minority classes of the DR stages; and 3) the classification being on a simplified
a clinical setting.

text: The HG-MEF-Bio fusion model had run 10 out of its intended 50 epochs when evaluated
at the interim point. Early stage training this far is not enough to accurately represent final
performance of a 50-epoch training, yet already validation accuracy 95.14% is a substantial
+4.51 pp over Architecture 1 after full 30-epoch training validation accuracy 90.63%,
validation Macro-F1 0.9278 vs 0.9057 (+0.0221). It’s also notable that all three of the best
checkpoints (bestbyaccuracy, bestbyF1, best_combined) yielded the same checkpoint file
weights for epoch 10 (each of 2,249.8MB) which indicated stable, coherent progress of
both accuracy and F1 objectives, with no indication of convergence between the two tasks
at this early stage. The spike of ~+1.2pp in validation accuracy from epoch 6 to epoch 10
directly followed the first DEFeatureMixer update (at epoch 6), suggesting that DE’s
updated expert feature scaling weight recalibration is indeed providing benefit to fusion
quality. By epoch 8 the ABC routing bias had been corrected to fix the AMD-to-Glaucoma
Expert routing failure seen with Architecture 1, recovering proper disease specific routing
for AMD and Cataract inputs. Given another 40 training epochs remaining, plus the PSO
based post-training threshold optimization yet to be performed, final performance metrics
for HG-MEF-Bio are expected to far exceed the values reported here at epoch 10 interim.

text: For all three experts the bio-inspired algorithms exhibited differing convergence
characteristic profiles: all three expert models showed instant convergence with the FA,
reaching near optimal EfficientNet-B4 channel attention values in the first iteration for
each respective training call (fitness ~0.045-0.067 for DR Bio, near-zero for AMD and
Glaucoma Bio due to saturation). This was further proof that the GradCAM spatial saliency
has a robust, non-ambiguous fitness signal for channel attention optimization. Most
illustrative for showing a trend relating the performance of the bio-algorithm to the quality
of the base model, the GWO demonstrated: the AMD Bio's GWO fitness was 1.0000 in
iteration 3 for every epoch update (ceiling effect); the Glaucoma Bio stabilized at 0.9375
after epoch 2; while the DR Bio went from early epoch values of 0.60-0.72 to values of
0.875-0.9375 at epoch 50. The GA appeared to have active minority class weight
exploration in the DR domain; all six runs demonstrated class weights ranging between
1.2-4.9 and confirm continued exploration of the penalty landscape, not premature
convergence. Although rapid fitness convergence occurred across all models in PSO, (~3.9,
~3.83 and 3.68-3.71 for AMD, Glaucoma, and DR, respectively) clinically distinguishable
threshold settings occurred: symmetrical for AMD, strongly asymmetric for Glaucoma
(NRG=0.101, RG=0.854) and multi-extreme for DR (Moderate=0.050 to
Proliferative=0.950).
All these experimental results highlight that the development of clinical deep learning
has been moving in the direction of trustworthy bio-inspired intelligent fusion, whereas
single model based approaches (in particular the Vision Transformer) achieved good
performances on overall classification tasks (approximately 90-91% on accuracy of DR
classification in Phase I) exceeding CNN baselines due to powerful global features
extraction, completely fail in classifying subtle clinically-important severity
distinctions of diseases; i.e. Classifying the sub-grades of diseases as aggregated
disease-classes. Therefore, the high performance of overall classification was a
misleading measurement of the actual worth of screening tool because the models were
unable to distinguish and classify the clinically-critical immediately-referable disease
classes (i.e. DR severity-Severe, glaucoma-referable), and the high accuracy on healthy
class among CNN baselines suggested that class imbalance is a significant confounding
Phase-II Architecture 1 addressed this limitation through disease-specific expert
specialization combined with hierarchical gated multi-expert fusion. The total
classification performance improved a lot as well and all the AMD, glaucoma and the
challenging 12-class merged problem also obtained good performance. But there is a
clinical limitation for this architecture. In the class balance-aware method, though
Severe DR achieved an outstanding AUC-ROC 0.980, it still gets an accuracy of 39.3%.
This means the model successfully extracted good features in the deep layers, but it
lacks the ability to adjust decision boundaries with such an imbalance scenario. So this
classifier would miss more than 60% of sight threatening DR patients in real world.
Through an further experiment, there were also bad signs about expert routing. For
example, AMD and Cataract images were still passed to the glaucoma expert though
the classification outcome was right. This seems to show that the model extract feature
in semantically-improper ways and is sensitive to the distribution shift.
Further confirmed this by Architecture 2 and effectively shows that by directly
embedding the bio-inspired algorithms into the training and optimization procedure,
drastic changes in the behavior of the model and medical usability occurred. With all
the algorithms including PSO, GA, GWO, ABC, DE all incorporated into the multi-
expert system with the Recall-Aware Diversity Loss, it can be seen that there is a
significant change in the accuracy from 39.3% to 92.8% for Severe DR and clearly
demonstrates that the error was not due to lack of learning visual features, but was an
issue with optimisation and calibration. Learning process in the presence of bio-inspired
optimization lead to more stable convergence and greater sensitivity towards minority
class and the learning algorithm was able to find medically relevant threshold values.
PSO optimization not only speeded up the learning process, it found decision thresholds
to be aligned with the medical triage process (emphasizing recall of the most critical
classes and conservatism towards others), GWO and DE optimized the cross-attention
fusion, and the lack of expertise coordination seen in architecture 1 was ameliorated
using the ABC algorithm. In conclusion, the results suggest that the proposed
biologically-inspired multi-expert fusion approach is an efficient, adaptable method
that can overcome the problems encountered by other deep learning approaches and
thus contribute to effective class imbalance, miscalibration, and inter-expert
synchronization for the application of intelligent screening of retinopathy in the field of
complex retinopathy diagnosis.
The following key findings were demonstrated through cross-phase and cross-
architecture comparisons:
• Specialisation per disease reduces inter-class feature interference : By
creating distinct specialist Phase-II experts for AMD, Glaucoma, and DR, we
showed an accuracy increase across domains, specifically +13.75 pp for AMD,
+17.45 pp for Glaucoma and +11.6 pp for DR, despite the phase exhibiting
significantly more categories than Phase I.
• The AUC-accuracy disparity : is due to unbalanced and miscalibrated
boundaries not a lack of representative features: The strong AUC-ROC for
DR_Severe in Architecture 1 was 0.980, but the argmax accuracy was just 37%
because the model correctly identified severity order but miscalibrated the
probabilities between grades. This validated the proposed PSO-based tuning of
per-class boundaries as the way to fix this issue.
• Bio-inspired algorithms complement traditional methods best where they
are weakest:The worst performing ( minority) classes of DR grades in
architecture 1, DRSevere (39.3% acc.), DRMild (63.6% acc.), and
DR_Proliferative (68.2% acc.), gained the largest improvements with bio-
inspired approaches (38.8+24.7=63.5 pp, 28.1 pp, 24.3 pp respectively),
whereas the highest performing DR grades showed no performance gain. This
supports their use as complements to gradient descent, not general performance
• Co-evolutionary bio-inspired training (SOL1) is better than simple
thresholding: In Architecture 2, by directly implementing the optimized PSO
thresholds as a penalty term in a during-training loss function, we observe a
smooth decrease in the validation loss of DR classification whereas in
architecture 1 this did not happen, with a steadily high loss until a point of
plateau; this was because the features themselves were being manipulated by
the PSO terms in training and not just a simple threshold manipulation.
• Benefit from GWO weight blending scales with base model : GWO benefits
the near-saturated AMD (1.0000 ceiling fitness), is a good complement for
moderate tasks (0.9375 on Glaucoma) and builds considerably on challenging
task performance (0.60 to 0.72, and finally to 0.875 to 0.9375 on DR). It appears
that GWO may have the most beneficial effect on the model when the minority
class performance need is highest in mid-training.
• PSO thresholds implement the clinical triage goals : The asymmetric
thresholds found for both the Glaucoma branch (NRG 0.101, RG 0.854) and the
DR branch (Severe 0.097, Proliferative 0.950) provide concrete representations
of clinical decision making to the model regarding false negatives and visually
represent the expressive capability of the FN-aware loss function (mean F1 +
3*mean Recall).
• The anomaly of the AMD expert within architecture 1 : This problem of
AMD expert utilization, although the task showed strong performance, is a
demonstration of the gating network converging to a local optimum, and not
that the AMD features themselves are poor; architecture 2 used a novel ABC-
based gating optimization and corrected this issue by epoch 8.
• Consistent improvement gain with the expert-then-fuse architecture with
bio-inspired fusion. Multi-disease accuracy increase on the overall average from
~90-91% of 4 abstracted classes (using Phase I ViT) up to 90.63% for the 12-
class Architectur1 HG-MEF, and then up to 95.14% (at epoch 10 of 50) for the
11-class Architectur2 HG-MEF-Bio.
• Joint multi-disease classification in a single pass inference.
• Leverage domain expertise without compromising on overall results.
• Specific addressing of minority class performance failure with biologically-
inspired solutions.
• Clinically interpretable outputs through gate weights and decision
• Scalable and modular.
• Highly robust, production quality training.
• Three-stage sequence training is painful.
• High computation load from six bio-inspired algorithms.
• Slight improvement of AMD regression in
CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts.
• HG-MEF-Bio fusion training is not completed at submission.
• Only tested on benchmark datasets, no further clinical verification done.
• Does not deal with multi-label comorbidity.
• PSO threshold tuning on validation set overfits the data.
• Genetic Algorithm fitness value does not accurately predict performance
in binary classification over small data sets.
In this thesis we design, implement and evaluate the Bio-Inspired Hierarchical Gating
Multi-Expert Fusion (HG-MEF-Bio) system to automate the classification of the 3 most
prevalent retinal diseases - Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD), Glaucoma and
Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) based on colour fundus photograph. The thesis was organized
into two project stages and two entire architectures where innovations are progressively
made at both stages, providing concrete and clinically useful gains.
This work's main architectural contribution is the expert-then-fuse approach. As the system
consists of three separately trained, disease-specific expert networks that are then fused
together using a learned hierarchical fusion network, the proposed method avoids inter-
class feature interference, which degrades naive, multi-disease, expert fusion. The
Architecture 1 HG-MEF baseline demonstrated that this paradigm yields specialist-level
accuracy across all three disease domains simultaneously: AMD at 97.75%, Glaucoma at
94.4%, and DR at 86.8% — substantially exceeding the Phase-I unified Vision
Transformer's performance on a significantly more demanding eleven-class taxonomy.
The six bio-inspired optimisation algorithms — Firefly Algorithm (FA), Grey Wolf
Optimiser (GWO), Genetic Algorithm (GA), Particle Swarm Optimisation (PSO),
Artificial Bee Colony (ABC), and Differential Evolution (DE) — were integrated as active
training-loop participants across every level of the Architecture 2 HG-MEF-Bio system.
The most clinically significant result of the entire research programme is the 53.5
percentage point improvement in Severe DR classification accuracy, rising from 39.3% in
Architecture 1 to 92.8% in Architecture 2 through the combined action of SOL1 (PSO in-
training threshold penalty), SOL2 (GA recall-floor constraint evolution), and SOL3
(Recall-Aware Diversity Loss). This is of direct patient safety relevance: a screening
mechanism correctly classifying 92.8% of Severe DR against the 39.3% accuracy of
Architecture 1 avoided many more cases of omitted referrals of patients for immediate
laser/anti-VEGF treatment which would otherwise result in irreversible loss of sight.
The end-to-end HG-MEF-Bio fusion model obtained a validation accuracy of 95.14% and
macro-F1 of 0.9278 at Epoch 10 of 50 of its training course - and at this stage already
bettered Architecture 1's 90.63% accuracy and 0.9057 F1 achieved after 30 full epochs.
The ABC-corrected routing network solved the AMD Expert under-utilization problem
identified in Architecture 1 and the DEFeatureMixer gave an instant +1.2 percentage point
accuracy improvement after it was applied for the first time at Epoch 6. The integration of
a differentiable Expected Calibration Error (ECE) loss at the fusion level represents the
first published application of training-time calibration regularisation in multi-disease
retinal classification, ensuring that the system's reported confidence levels are statistically
reliable for clinical decision support. These outcomes taken together support the main
hypothesis that, when directly built into, rather than attached as tuners to the training-loop,
bio-inspired algorithms can overcome precisely the failure cases which pure gradient-based
learning with fixed weights and fixed augmentations fails to solve (minority class
imbalance, route collapse and incorrectly calibrated decisions). To summarize, we've
shown a monotonic, architecture driven path from ~90% unifying accuracy over 4 broad
disease categories (Phase-I ViT) to 95.14% intermediate accuracy over 11 detailed clinical
gradations (Architecture 2 HG-MEF-Bio), and developed a justified, interpretable and
clinically extensible approach to population scale, AI driven retinal disease screening.
Despite the advantages of the system, some important directions of future research are
evident from both the success and failures obtained from this work. They are as follows.

text: Objectives The aim of the study is to emphasize and explore the possible transtemporal approaches for spectrum of complicated lateral skull base pathologies. Design Retrospective analysis of complicated lateral skull base pathologies was managed in our institute between January 2017 and December 2019. Setting The study was conducted in a tertiary care referral center. Main Outcome Measures The study focused on the selection of approach based on site and extent of the pathology, the surgical nuances for each approach, and the associated complications. Results A total of 10 different pathologies of the lateral skull base were managed by different transtemporal approaches. The most common complication encountered was facial nerve palsy (43%, n ¼ 6). Other complications included cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) collection (15%, n ¼ 2), cosmetic deformity (24%, n ¼ 4), petrous internal carotid artery injury (7%, n ¼ 1), and hypoglossal nerve palsy (7%, n ¼ 1). The cosmetic deformity included flap necrosis (n ¼ 2) and postoperative bony defects leading to contour defects of the scalp (n ¼ 2). Conclusion Surgical approach should be tailored based on the individual basis, to obtain adequate exposure and complete excision. Selection of appropriate surgical approach should also be based on the training and preference of the operating surgeon. Whenever necessary, combined surgical approaches facilitating full tumor exposure are recommended so that complete tumor excision is feasible. This requires a multidisciplinary team comprising neurosurgeons, neuro-otologist, neuroanesthetist, and plastic surgeons. The surgeon must know precise microsurgical anatomy to preserve the adjacent nerves and vessels, which is necessary for better surgical outcomes.

text: The anatomy of the temporal bone, its complex, intimate, and intricate anatomical relationship to the skull base structures makes the management of the lesions in the vicinity very challenging. The temporal bone has five parts: squamosal, petrous, mastoid, tympanic, and styloid process. Temporal bone pathologies usually present with symptoms of hearing deficit (conductive, sensorineural, mixed), vestibular dysfunction, facial nerve dysfunction, mastication difficulties, and dysphagia. Imaging plays an essential role in the determination of the exact location of the lesion along with the relationship of the lesion with surrounding neurovascular structures and may suggest the differential diagnosis of pathologies. Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are often complementary to each other, and in most cases, both are required. To evaluate the relationship of the internal carotid artery (ICA) with the tumor/lesion, magnetic resonance angiography or digital subtraction angiogram is considered often.

text: A surgical approach is defined as the route taken for the surgical procedure from an opening to the target. Various approaches are currently available for the management of temporal bone pathologies. 1, 2 Usually, two or more approaches are combined for the same lesion; therefore, intimate knowledge of anatomy and multidisciplinary evaluation are essential factors to be considered in choosing an appropriate approach for this complex area. This ensures both effective treatment of pathology and better functional and cosmetic outcomes. The knowledge of the structures we encounter in any particular approach is vital along with the judgment of which are to be preserved, mobilized, or removed. It determines the success of choosing the particular surgical corridor for particular lesion and accessibility. The selection of the approach used depends upon the type of pathology whether benign or malignant, site of origin, and extension which may be confined to temporal bone or extending to the adjacent areas of the neck, infratemporal fossa, and in the "exo" and "endo" cranial regions or both. Rhoton Jr 2 classified the temporal approaches into three categories. It is essential to consider multiple factors during the surgical planning to get a good functional outcome, which is cosmetically appealing with minimal morbidity at the end. It includes proper skin flap design without compromising its vascularity, especially while doing the revision cases. Proper dissection and preservation of muscle and musculoperiosteal flap are also important to ensure a tight cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) closure as well as obliteration of the surgical cavity at the end of surgery. The approach should give adequate exposure and straight-line access to the pathology with minimal to no brain retraction and be versatile enough to expand intraoperatively. The need for preoperative embolization and intraoperative measures to tackle blood loss is planned well before the intervention. The present review enumerates the challenging case scenarios that we have managed through the transtemporal approaches.

text: Extended mastoidectomy is performed using microsurgical cutting and diamond burr with continuous suction and irrigation. The initial step was by using postauricular incision; skin flaps and musculoperiosteal flap were raised; outer mastoid cortex air cells were drilled out followed by opening of the mastoid antrum and identification of the lateral semicircular canal, which is the most reliable landmark in the temporal bone and helps in the identification of facial nerve and bony labyrinth. Bone is removed from the sinodural angle and along the superior petrosal sinus. The mastoid air cells are exenterated from the sinodural angle, tegmen, and posterior fossa dural plate areas.

text: A 55-year-old gentleman is a known case of left vestibular schwannoma, he underwent left Retro-mastoid-sub-occipital (RMSO) craniectomy and excision of the tumor 11 years ago. During that surgery the left eighth cranial nerve was sacrificed, while the left seventh cranial nerve was preserved. Now, he presented with left hemi-facial spasm and left-sided gait ataxia, on MRI there was an evidence of recurrence of the lesion for which he underwent re-exploration of left RMSO craniectomy and gross total excision recurrence was done. Two months after the second surgery, he came with complaints of watery discharge from the nose. CT cisternography showed a CSF tract from the operated cavity filling the mastoid cavity through the supra labyrinthine tract into the middle ear and through the Eustachian tube into the nasal cavity. The patient was planned for extended cortical mastoidectomy and repair of the fistulous tract. The left postauricular incision was made followed by extended cortical mastoidectomy. Tegmen, posterior fossa dural plate, labyrinthine block, and sigmoid sinus were delineated and preserved. CSF leak through the supralabyrinthine cell tract was identified (►Fig. 1A and B) and demarked to be reconstructed with musculoperiosteal tissue and fat. Aditus was blocked with fat. Fibrin glue was applied (►Fig. 1C).

text: Extended cortical mastoidectomy is the preferred approach in cases where hearing preservation is required. However, there are many situations where hearing is already lost, and the pathology involves the middle ear cleft where a more radical approach is needed in the form of radical mastoidectomy. The difference between a radical mastoidectomy and extended cortical mastoidectomy is that the posterior canal wall was taken down along with the removal of middle ear structures like ossicles (except stapes footplate) along with the obliteration of Eustachian tube opening into the middle ear. The facial nerve within the fallopian canal was delineated and preserved.

text: Temporal Bone Hemangioma A 2.5-year-old male child presented with a history of right ear bleeding and discharge with a mass in external auditory canal (EAC). Clinical evaluation showed a fleshy mass in the right EAC, with the normal facial nerve. CT scan showed evidence of soft tissue density filling the EAC, middle ear, and mastoid antrum. MRI showed an evidence of contrast-enhancing lesion filling the mastoid (►Fig. 1D) and EAC. Possibility of rhabdomyosarcoma was suspected because of the presenting age. The patient was planned for radical mastoidectomy. Through a post aural incision, cortical mastoidectomy was done; tegmen and sigmoid sinus plate were identified, and the mastoid tip was removed. A highly vascular mass was noted, filling the mastoid cavity and involving the middle ear (►Fig. 1E). This was gradually debulked with cautery. During dissection, the disease was found involving the tympanic and mastoid segment of the facial nerve. The involved segment was resected, and the cut end was anastomosed using the greater auricular nerve graft. The histopathology showed hemangioma; hence the possible site of origin of hemangioma was thought to be facial nerve.

text: Radical mastoidectomy is chosen in cases where the petrous apex/bony labyrinth is spared. However, in cases with the disease involving the middle ear cleft but extending into the labyrinth or a primary disease of the petrous bone with hearing loss, a transcochlear approach can be used. The transcochlear approach is mainly useful for lesion involving the petrous apex and adjoining areas with hearing loss. House and Hitselberger have initially described the transcochlear approach; it includes identification of the internal auditory canal, posterior rerouting of the facial nerve, and removal of the cochlea and petrous apex with the preservation of middle ear and EAC 3 . In modified transcochlear approach, we combine the removal of the middle ear and external auditory canal with posterior re-routing of the facial nerve; this widens the exposure and allows better control of the temporal carotid artery and ease the complete removal of petrous apex lesion. 4 We had two rare cases involving the temporal bone, (1) Petrous apex recurrent chondrosarcoma and (2) Fibrous dysplasia of temporal bone which were managed by the modified transcochlear approach.

text: A 45-year-old female presented with complaints of neck mass with headache, who had undergone surgery 4 years back and was a histologically proven case of petrous chondrosarcoma. text: A 21-yearold male presented with right-sided painless swelling behind the ear with ear discharge for 4 years. He had undergone two surgeries for the same complaints in the past 8 years. After the second surgery he developed facial nerve palsy. The histopathology showed fibrous dysplasia. CT showed a well-defined lytic lesion replacing the entire temporal bone, with the displacement of the cerebellum. MRI showed well-defined large nonenhancing lesion involving the right temporal bone with significant compression on the intracranial structures (►Fig. 2E). Due to multiple recurrences, we planned for a radical excision. A right craniotemporocervical incision was made (►Fig. 2F), and the tumor was gradually debulked and separated from the middle fossa dura. As the tumor was densely adherent to the posterior fossa dura, during resection, there was rent in the dura, which was repaired using artificial dura. Due to multiple surgeries, there was skin flap necrosis, which was managed nonsurgically. Cranioplasty was planned at a later stage.
